warmup.q: The company's own account, number 900, has four lines at exactly 9:00 on 2 January: -100000, -80000, -30000 and -140000. (The app keeps money in cents, so -100000 is -1,000.00.) The balance column is sum(amount_minor) OVER (ORDER BY created_at), which adds up the amounts in time order. What does it show on the first of the four lines?
options: -100000, the first amount on its own
NULL, the database's word for no value, because nobody said which of the four came first
One of -100000, -180000, -210000 or -350000, and which one can change from run to run
warmup.why: With an ORDER BY and nothing else, the sum reads every row from the start up to the current row, plus every row that ties with it on the time. All four lines say 9:00, so each one adds up all four: -350000. The first section shows why PostgreSQL works this way. The first option is what most people expect, because "running total" sounds like one row at a time. The last option is what you get once you tell it to count single rows but give it nothing to break the tie with: then the order of the four is up to the database.

sections.h: Why four lines show one balance: the default frame takes in ties
sections.html:
First, where the statement comes from. The app keeps its data in PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run. A database keeps data in tables, like sheets in a spreadsheet: each row is one record, and each column holds one piece of it. You ask it questions in SQL, the language most databases understand.

One table, ledger_entries, is the app's ledger: the list of every movement of money. Each row is one entry, with the account it touches, the amount in cents and the time (created_at). Every movement is written twice, so money never appears from nowhere. When a customer puts 1,000.00 into their account, a deposit, the ledger gets +100000 on their account and -100000 on account 900. That's the company's own account, which stands for money coming in from outside, so its balance goes down with every deposit. Here's the start of its statement:

 entry_id | amount_minor |       created_at       | balance
----------+--------------+------------------------+---------
        2 |      -100000 | 2026-01-02 09:00:00+00 | -350000
        4 |       -80000 | 2026-01-02 09:00:00+00 | -350000
        6 |       -30000 | 2026-01-02 09:00:00+00 | -350000
        8 |      -140000 | 2026-01-02 09:00:00+00 | -350000
       16 |       -50000 | 2026-01-10 09:00:00+00 | -405000
       18 |        -5000 | 2026-01-10 09:00:00+00 | -405000

The first line should say -100000: one deposit so far. Instead, four lines show -350000, the balance after all four, and on 10 January it happens again. The balance column is sum(amount_minor) OVER (ORDER BY created_at), and this is exactly what it means.

A window function computes a value for each row from a set of other rows, and keeps every row. OVER (...) says which rows, and ORDER BY created_at inside it puts them in time order. Then sum adds up the rows from the first one to the current one: a running total. To be exact, each call reads a frame: the rows it actually looks at for the current row.

Picture the statement's lines as paper receipts in a pile, sorted by time. You slide a card with a slot cut in it down the pile. For each receipt, what shows through the slot is its frame, and sum adds up what it sees. The receipt is the row, the order of the pile is the ORDER BY, and the slot is the frame.

You can cut the slot yourself, with a frame clause after the ORDER BY. If you don't, PostgreSQL cuts one for you: RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, from the first row up to the current row. RANGE cuts by the value you sort on, the time printed on the receipt. Four receipts that say 9:00 on 2 January can't be told apart by time, so the slot shows all four or none. Rows that tie on the ORDER BY value are called peers. For entry 2, the frame runs from the first row to its last peer, entry 8, and the sum is -350000. Entries 4, 6 and 8 get the same frame and the same sum.

The same rule explains the last lesson's plain totals. Without an ORDER BY, every row is a peer of every other, so the frame is the whole partition, the set of rows the window works in. With ties, the running total moves in jumps, one per set of peers.

There are two fixes, and you usually want both. Make the ORDER BY unique by adding a column that never repeats: ORDER BY created_at, entry_id. Then no row has a peer, and the slot ends exactly at the current row. Or cut the slot by counting rows: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. ROWS alone stops the jump, but PostgreSQL still decides which of the four tied rows comes first, so the balances between them can move from run to run. The tiebreaker fixes the order, and writing ROWS too tells the next reader what you meant.

Rows that can tie will tie. End a window's ORDER BY with a unique column. Each batch's last line was right all along, so a check of the final balance alone never sees the bug.

So far, the slot has run from the start to the current row. Next, we'll cut it seven days wide, and find that seven rows and seven days aren't the same thing.

try.title: Watch a running total jump
steps: Start the database from the labs folder if it isn't running: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait. This runs PostgreSQL inside Docker, a program that runs separate small machines, called containers, on your computer. Then open psql, PostgreSQL's command line, where you type SQL and see the answer: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course.
Run the query below. It prints the first seven entries of account 900 with three balance columns: the default frame, a ROWS frame, and a unique ORDER BY. Compare them on the first six rows.
Look at rows_seen, which counts the rows in each default frame with count(*). Why does the first row say 4?
Remove entry_id from the ORDER BY of the tiebreak column and run it again. Which column does it match now?

code.title: psql, database course

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18: Window function calls (frames and peers)

aside.title: Why doesn't PostgreSQL keep tied rows in the order they arrived?
aside.html: Because a table has no order of its own. The relational model, keys and NULL showed that a table is a bag of rows: PostgreSQL stores a new row wherever it finds room, and a change to a row can move it. When it sorts by created_at, rows with the same time can come out in any order, and that order can change between runs. The only order you can count on is the one you write in ORDER BY. If entry_id should decide, write it there.

sections.h: Seven rows or seven days: ROWS, RANGE and GROUPS
sections.html:
The company wants a 7-day sales line for March: for each day, the money taken that day and in the six days before it. Card payments live in another table, payments, one row per payment. Each row has the shop it paid (merchant_id, because the app calls shops merchants), the amount in cents and the time. Its status is succeeded when the money moved, and failed when the card was declined.

First, fold the payments into one row per day with GROUP BY, which sorts rows into groups and turns each group into one row. Then put a window over the day rows. The small test data has sales on only seven March days: the 1st, 4th, 8th, 12th, 15th, 25th and 31st.

A frame clause has a unit, a start and an end:

{ ROWS | RANGE | GROUPS } BETWEEN start AND end
start, end:  UNBOUNDED PRECEDING | n PRECEDING | CURRENT ROW | n FOLLOWING | UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING

PRECEDING means before the current row, FOLLOWING means after it, and UNBOUNDED means all the way to the edge of the partition.

The first attempt counts rows. ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is the current row and the six rows before it. For 8 March it adds the 1st, 4th and 8th: 100810. But the 1st is seven days back, outside the week. On 31 March it adds all seven rows, the whole month: 211132. Six rows back isn't six days back when most days have no row.

RANGE measures by value instead, the way the default did with times. RANGE BETWEEN interval '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW takes every row whose day is at most six days before the current row's day. (An interval is a length of time, such as '6 days'.) On 8 March that's the 4th and the 8th, 36810. On 31 March it's the 25th and the 31st, 53325. A RANGE with a distance needs exactly one ORDER BY column, of a type you can subtract from: a number, or a date or time with an interval.

GROUPS counts sets of peers. GROUPS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, over payments sorted by day, takes the current row's day and the day with payments before it, however many rows each holds. It's the rarest of the three, for "this batch and the one before". In the receipt picture, ROWS counts receipts, RANGE reads the date printed on them, and GROUPS counts the little piles of receipts that share a date.

One more tool: a calendar turns ROWS back into days: SELECT date '2026-03-01' + n AS day FROM generate_series(0, 30) AS n makes one row for each day of March, from the numbers 0 to 30. Join the daily totals onto it with a LEFT JOIN, which keeps every day even when no payment matches. Now every day is a row, the days with no sales too, which an average per calendar day needs.

Last, a trap from the order a query runs in. PostgreSQL runs FROM (which tables to read), then WHERE (which rows to keep), then GROUP BY, and only then the window functions (The relational model, keys and NULL). So if WHERE keeps only March payments, the window never sees the February days that the first week of March needs. Read the extra six days in, compute the window, and keep only March in a query around it.

The receipt picture breaks in one place. You'd add up the whole slot again for every receipt. For sums and counts, PostgreSQL keeps a running sum instead: it adds the row that enters the frame and takes off the row that leaves. Next, we'll ask for the frame's last row instead of its sum, and get an answer that looks broken.

sections.h: Asking for the smallest payment: last_value and where the frame ends
sections.html:
The team that watches for stolen cards wants every payment shown next to its shop's biggest and smallest succeeded payment, to see how far each one sits from the extremes. Two window functions look made for it: first_value(x) returns x from the first row of the frame, and last_value(x) from the last row. Sort each shop's payments biggest first, and first_value should be the biggest and last_value the smallest:

SELECT merchant_id, payment_id, amount_minor,
       first_value(amount_minor) OVER w AS largest,
       last_value(amount_minor)  OVER w AS smallest
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'succeeded'
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY merchant_id ORDER BY amount_minor DESC);

PARTITION BY merchant_id gives each shop its own partition, and a frame never leaves its partition. WINDOW w AS (...) names the window once, so both functions can use it.

first_value is right on every row. last_value is wrong on almost every row. At Volt Electronics, an electronics shop, it shows each payment's own amount: 129900 next to 129900, 75000 next to 75000. At Metro Transit, which sells bus and train rides, it shows 550 for the 5.50 ride and 275 for the 2.75 rides, which looks right for the wrong reason.

The frame explains it. The window has an ORDER BY and no frame clause, so it gets the default frame from the first section. That runs from the start of the partition to the current row's last peer. The last row of that frame is the current row, or its last peer when there's a tie. That's why the three 275 rides show 275: they are peers, and the frame reaches the last of them. first_value works only because the default frame starts at the start. The PostgreSQL documentation, to its credit, warns that the default frame "is likely to give unhelpful results for last_value".

There are three fixes. Give last_value the whole partition with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. Or reverse the order and use first_value. Or, for a plain smallest value, use min(amount_minor) OVER (PARTITION BY merchant_id) with no ORDER BY at all, so the frame is the whole shop. nth_value(x, 2), the value from the frame's second row, has the same trap. On a partition's first row the frame holds one row, and the second isn't in it yet, so you get NULL, the database's word for no value.

A named window can take a frame on top: OVER (w ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) copies w's PARTITION BY and ORDER BY and adds the frame.

Why did the ranks of the last lesson never go wrong like this? Not every window function reads the frame. Aggregates with OVER read it (functions such as sum, count and avg, which fold many values into one), and so do first_value, last_value and nth_value. The ranking functions row_number, rank and dense_rank ignore it, and so do lag and lead, which read the row before or after. They work on the whole partition in window order. That's why lag(x) is NULL on a partition's first row, whatever frame you write.

A function that reads the frame needs the frame you meant. Write it out.

Next, we'll stop looking at the rows near one row and look for runs of rows, which GROUP BY can't see.

sections.h: Three failed logins in a row: number the rows twice and subtract
sections.html:
The app also records every attempt to log in. A third table, login_events, gets one row per attempt, with the customer and the time (occurred_at). It also says whether the password was right (success, true or false) and which internet address the attempt came from. The security team wants to lock an account after three failed logins in a row. First, they want to see every run of failures, per customer, with its length.

Here's Elena's history (customer 5): two successes, six failures in two minutes from an address she had never used, 203.0.113.7, then her own success. It looks like someone guessing her password.

success:  t  t  f  f  f  f  f  f  t

A run of equal values with no other value between them is called an island, and the places where the value changes are the gaps. Elena has three islands: two successes, six failures, one success. The shape turns up often, as in declined payments in a row or days in a row with sales. In the receipt picture, islands are runs of receipts of one colour.

GROUP BY is the first thing to try, and it can't work. GROUP BY customer_id, success puts Elena's three successes in one group, though they belong to two islands. Jonas (customer 10) is worse off. He failed twice in April and twice in June, with a success after each pair. GROUP BY counts four failures and would lock him out, though he never failed three times in a row. GROUP BY sees which rows share a value. It can't see whether they sit next to each other.

The trick is to number the rows twice with row_number(), a window function that numbers the rows of a partition 1, 2, 3 in window order. First, number all of a customer's logins in time order. Then number them again, separately for successes and for failures. Inside an island, both numbers go up by one per row, so their difference stays the same. Between two islands of the same outcome, the first counter keeps counting through the other outcome's rows while the second doesn't, so the next island gets a bigger difference.

Elena's failures have overall numbers 3 to 8 and failure numbers 1 to 6: the difference is 2 on all six. Her first two successes have a difference of 0. Her last success is overall number 9 and success number 3, so its difference is 6. The difference names the island, so call it the island id. Group by customer, outcome and island id, and each island folds into one row with a count, a first time and a last time.

Two details decide whether this works. Number all the logins first, and only then keep the failures. If WHERE keeps only failures before the numbering, every failure sits next to the previous failure in the numbered list, and Jonas's two pairs become one island of four. And an island id is unique only within one customer and one outcome, because a success island and a failure island can get the same number. So group by the outcome as well, or keep only the failures after the numbering.

The two counters take "in a row" to mean "the next row". Sometimes it means "soon after". Next, we'll draw the gaps by time.

sections.h: Sessions and sales streaks: when the gap is measured in time
sections.html:
A login session is a burst of logins less than 10 minutes apart. A sales streak is a run of days with no day missing. Both are islands, but the gap that ends them is measured in time, so the two counters can't find them.

Build them in two steps. First, mark each row that starts a new island with a 1, and every other row with a 0. A login starts a session if more than 10 minutes passed since the customer's previous login, or if there's no previous login. lag(x), from the last lesson, reads x from the row before in the same partition. Then number the islands with a running total of the marks. Each 1 adds one, so all the rows up to the next 1 carry the same number.

WITH flagged AS (
    SELECT customer_id, event_id, occurred_at,
           CASE WHEN occurred_at - lag(occurred_at) OVER w <= interval '10 minutes'
                THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS starts_session
    FROM login_events
    WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id)
)
SELECT customer_id, event_id, occurred_at,
       sum(starts_session) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id) AS session
FROM flagged;

WITH flagged AS (...) gives the first step a name, so the query below can read from it like a table. CASE WHEN ... THEN 0 ELSE 1 END is SQL's if-else. A customer's first login has no login before it, so lag returns NULL. A comparison with NULL is never true, so CASE falls through to ELSE and starts a new session.

Elena gets three sessions: 20 January, 19:40 on 6 March, and the burst that starts at 19:52. Her success at 19:58 comes 4 minutes 20 seconds after the last failure, so it joins the attacker's session. With a 2-minute rule, it would start a fourth.

The query needs two levels because a window function can't take another window function's result as input at the same level. sum(lag(x) OVER w) OVER v fails with window function calls cannot be nested. The inner level computes the marks, and the level around it adds them up.

For whole days, the row-number trick from the last section works on dates directly. Take the days with sales, number them in order, and subtract the number from the date: day - row_number() OVER (ORDER BY day)::int. On days in a row, the date and the number both go up by one, so the result stays the same date. A missing day makes it jump. On the course's large data set, a generated copy of the tables with a million payments, shop 1000 had sales on 160 of 300 days. Its longest streak was six days, 6 to 11 May.

In a language like Kotlin, both methods are one loop with a counter that starts a new group whenever the value changes or the gap is too big. A query has no variable that lives on from one row to the next, so SQL carries information across rows with window functions instead.

These tools find only runs of one value, or runs broken by one kind of gap. A pattern like "two failures, then a success from a new address" gets awkward fast. Oracle, another database program, can describe patterns over rows directly; PostgreSQL 18 can't, and the comparison in this lesson shows both. And every window sorts the rows it covers, so on a big table these queries cost at least that sort.

opening:
Picture a small company that runs a payments app. People pay for coffee, books and groceries with a card, and the app records each payment. One January morning, you're asked for a statement of the company's own account: every movement of money, with the balance right after it, like a bank statement.

You write the query, the question you ask the database, and run it. The first four lines look wrong. Four customers put money in at exactly 9:00 on 2 January, and the balance doesn't step along with the amounts.

The query is the running total from Window functions: ranking, LAG and running totals, and it passed every test. That's the trap. Test data written by hand has a different time on every row, but real money often arrives in batches that share one time.

In this lesson, we'll find out which rows a window function reads for each row, and choose them on purpose. Then we'll use the same tools to find a streak of failed logins. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a statement whose first four lines showed one balance. The default frame takes in every row that ties with the current one, so a batch of deposits at 9:00 shared one total. A column that never repeats fixed it, and the same tools found Elena's six failed logins in a row.

Open the list of payments in your bank's app. Find two payments in the same minute, and check whether the balance steps once for each or jumps over both.

Next, we'll ask for a few rows per group instead of a value per row: each shop's three biggest sales. Then we'll find out why page 5,001 of a long list is so slow.

compare.title: Streaks of three or more failures: Oracle's MATCH_RECOGNIZE and PostgreSQL's islands

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle, MATCH_RECOGNIZE (12c and later)
a.html: SELECT customer_id, failures, first_at, last_at FROM login_events MATCH_RECOGNIZE ( PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id MEASURES COUNT(*) AS failures, FIRST(occurred_at) AS first_at, LAST(occurred_at) AS last_at ONE ROW PER MATCH PATTERN (f{3,}) -- three or more f rows in a row DEFINE f AS success = FALSE -- BOOLEAN columns: Oracle 23ai and later );

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL 18, number twice and group
b.html: WITH numbered AS ( SELECT customer_id, occurred_at, success, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id) - row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id, success ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id) AS island FROM login_events ) SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS failures, min(occurred_at) AS first_at, max(occurred_at) AS last_at FROM numbered WHERE NOT success GROUP BY customer_id, island HAVING count(*) >= 3;

compare.note: Both find Elena's six failures. Oracle is another database program, sold by the company of the same name and run by many banks and large firms. Its MATCH_RECOGNIZE, from the 2016 edition of the SQL standard (the shared rule book that makers of databases follow), describes the streak as a pattern over rows, a little like a search pattern over text. PATTERN names a sequence of kinds of row, DEFINE says what each kind means, and MEASURES computes values over each match. It reads closer to the question, and it handles patterns that are awkward with window functions, such as "two failures, then a success from a new address". PostgreSQL 18 has no MATCH_RECOGNIZE, so the same question is written with two row_numbers and a GROUP BY, or with lag marks and a running sum. A query moved from Oracle to PostgreSQL needs that rewrite by hand. Older Oracle tables keep true and false as a number or a letter, so their DEFINE reads success = 0 or success = 'N'.

worked.title: From failure streaks to how long each attack lasted

steps.say: The security team also wants to know how long each streak of three or more failures went on before the customer got in again. Start from the island numbering of the fourth section, over every customer and both outcomes. The success islands are needed too: the one after a failure island says when the customer got back in.
steps.code: -- 1. number every login twice: the difference is the island id WITH numbered AS ( SELECT customer_id, event_id, occurred_at, success, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id) - row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id, success ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id) AS island FROM login_events ),

steps.say: Fold each island into one row. The GROUP BY includes success, because island ids repeat across outcomes. At the same level, a window can run over the grouped rows, as in Window functions: ranking, LAG and running totals. lead(x) reads x from the row after, so lead(min(occurred_at)) is the start of the customer's next island, with the islands sorted by their own starts.
steps.code: -- 2. one row per island, and the start of the island after it islands AS ( SELECT customer_id, success, count(*) AS attempts, min(occurred_at) AS first_at, max(occurred_at) AS last_at, lead(min(occurred_at)) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY min(occurred_at)) AS next_island_at FROM numbered GROUP BY customer_id, success, island )

steps.say: Now keep the failure islands of three or more. This filter must sit one level up: inside islands, it would remove the success islands before lead could look at them. After a failure island, the next island is always a success, so next_island_at is the next successful login. It's NULL when the customer never logged in again.
steps.code: -- 3. filter after the window has seen every island SELECT customer_id, attempts, first_at, last_at, next_island_at, next_island_at - first_at AS until_next_success FROM islands WHERE NOT success AND attempts >= 3 ORDER BY customer_id, first_at;

steps.say: One streak in the test data: Elena's six failures, and her own success six minutes after the first one. Jonas's islands have two failures each, so the filter drops them, which is the point of counting in a row.

answer.html: SELECT success, count(*) AS attempts, min(occurred_at) AS first_at, max(occurred_at) AS last_at FROM (SELECT occurred_at, success, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id) -- all logins - row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY success ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id) AS island -- per outcome FROM login_events WHERE customer_id = 10) AS numbered GROUP BY success, island -- island ids repeat across outcomes, so group by both ORDER BY first_at; -- f | 2 | 2026-04-19 12:10:00 | 2026-04-19 12:11:00 -- t | 1 | 2026-04-19 12:12:00 | 2026-04-19 12:12:00 -- f | 2 | 2026-06-08 07:30:00 | 2026-06-08 07:30:40 -- t | 1 | 2026-06-08 07:31:30 | 2026-06-08 07:31:30 -- With NOT success in the inner WHERE, the successes are gone before the numbering, both -- counters move together on every failure, and all four failures become one island.

recap: A window function's frame is the set of rows it reads for the current row. With an ORDER BY and no frame clause, it runs from the partition's first row to the current row, and takes in every row tied with it.
Rows that tie on the ORDER BY are peers, and they share one running total. End the ORDER BY with a column that never repeats, and write ROWS when you mean rows.
ROWS counts rows, RANGE measures the sorted value (interval '6 days' PRECEDING), and GROUPS counts sets of peers. When days are missing, rows aren't days.
last_value and nth_value read the frame, and the default frame ends at the current row. Give them the whole partition, or use first_value, min or max.
Islands: row_number over all rows minus row_number within each value stays the same inside a run. For gaps in time, mark each start with lag and add the marks up.
The limit: these tools find runs of one value or one kind of gap. Richer patterns over rows need a feature PostgreSQL 18 doesn't have, and every window costs a sort of the rows it covers.

explain.prompt: A screen shows a running total of daily deposits that sometimes jumps by two deposits at once, and a "balance at the end of the month" column, written with last_value, that only repeats each row's own balance. Explain both bugs to a friend, using the word frame, and fix them.
explain.answer: Both come from the default frame. A window function reads a frame, the rows it looks at for each row. With an ORDER BY and no frame clause, that's RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, and in RANGE mode the current row takes in all its peers, the rows with the same ORDER BY value. Two deposits with the same time are peers, so each one's running total already includes the other, and the total jumps by both at once. The fix is a unique ORDER BY, such as the time and then the deposit's id, plus ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW to say it plainly. last_value returns the last row of the frame, and the default frame ends at the current row, so it returns the current row's own balance. To get the month's last balance, give it the whole month: PARTITION BY month with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. Or take first_value with the order reversed.

deeper.html:
The frame clause has one more part: it can leave rows out. After the end you can write EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW (drop the current row), EXCLUDE GROUP (drop the current row and its peers), EXCLUDE TIES (drop the peers but keep the current row) or EXCLUDE NO OTHERS, the default. So avg(amount_minor) OVER (PARTITION BY merchant_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW) is the average of the same shop's other payments. That's the fair thing to compare a suspicious payment with, because a big payment would pull its own average up. EXCLUDE GROUP is how you compare a payment with the other days, not with payments made at the same moment.

Frames are cheap for some functions and not for others. For sum, count and avg, PostgreSQL can keep a running result and, when a row leaves a moving frame such as 6 PRECEDING, subtract it instead of adding up the whole frame again. The documentation calls this moving-aggregate mode, and it needs an inverse function: a way to undo one row. min and max have no inverse, so a sliding maximum over a large frame looks through the frame again each time the old maximum leaves it. On frames of a few rows the difference doesn't matter; on a 10,000-row sliding frame it does.

RANGE has a cost of its own. To know where the current row's peers end, PostgreSQL has to look ahead past the current row. ROWS doesn't. That's why EXPLAIN, the command that shows how PostgreSQL plans to run a query, often shows ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING for functions that don't depend on the frame: the planner, the part of PostgreSQL that picks how to run a query, switches to the cheaper mode when the result can't change.

The two-counter trick works for any value that defines "the same run". Put it in the second PARTITION BY: the status of an order, the internet address of a login, the shop of a payment. And a run can follow more than one rule at once, for example "failures from the same address with less than a minute between them". Combine a lag mark for the time gap with a mark for a change of address, and add up either.

Oracle and the 2016 SQL standard have row pattern recognition, MATCH_RECOGNIZE, for patterns richer than a run of one value. PostgreSQL 18 doesn't have it, so the techniques in this lesson are what you use instead.
